headline: Banking's center of gravity moves to identity, real-time data and governed AI by 2030
thesis: By 2030 banking is re-organizing around a handful of perimeters — identity, real-time payments data, financial-crime/fraud AI under governance, and operational resilience — where regulation seeds much of the demand but competitive value is won in how fast and how widely the rails are operated; the customer-facing infrastructure is increasingly bought by non-banks, and the physical cash estate is the smallest, slowest-moving part of the story. The lightbulb: the durable money is not in any single mandate but in operating the shared, regulated rails — verification, real-time fraud, data products, resilience — as managed services across many markets and a buyer base far wider than banks.
picture: The shape of demand inverts. Identity becomes platform infrastructure rather than a one-off onboarding cost: EUDI wallets must be issued by every Member State by 6 Dec 2026 and accepted by all regulated relying parties for ID and SCA by 6 Dec 2027, while the AML Regulation lands 10 Jul 2027 — turning verification into a recurring, cryptographically-anchored defence as deepfake fraud (Deloitte: ~USD 40bn of US GenAI-fraud losses by 2027, from USD 12.3bn in 2023) breaks legacy eKYC. Payments go instant-by-default — non-euro CEE PSPs bound to SCT Inst and Verification-of-Payee by 9 Jul 2027, EU instant volume ~10x from ~3bn (2024) to ~30bn by 2028 — so value migrates up the stack: not to clearing, but to verification, real-time fraud orchestration and ISO 20022 DATA PRODUCTS, where structured-payment data becomes a sold P&L (cash-flow forecasting, liquidity and treasury analytics), not just a migration artifact. AI moves from copilot to operator, with banking AI software spend rising EUR 31bn (2024) to EUR 55bn (2027) and agentic AI embedded in ~33% of enterprise apps by 2028.

The money and the buyers both move. Identity-verification (~15-17% CAGR to USD 29-34bn by 2030), digital signature (31-39% CAGR), AML (USD 4.1bn to 9.4bn), RegTech (USD 21bn to 44bn by 2030) and the fraud-detection pool (USD 32bn to ~66bn by 2030) all compound on legislated or loss-driven clocks, not discretionary budgets — and the buyer is increasingly NOT a retail-banking channels team but the CRO, CISO, CDO, model-risk and compliance functions, plus an entirely new non-bank class. PSD3/PSR (in force ~2027) and FIDA (phasing 2027-2030) legitimize the licensed FISP, while the amended Settlement Finality Directive (plus the 2025 EBA/ECB/NCB MoU) grants payment institutions/EMIs direct TARGET2/TIPS access, and embedded finance scales Europe's revenue pool toward EUR 100bn+ by 2030, B2B-dominated. A caution sits under all of it: regulators routinely slip — the EUDI clock itself may drift to ~2032 — so demand timing, not demand existence, is the live risk, and the winners hedge by selling readiness rather than betting on dates landing on schedule.

The endgame is structural, not cyclical. Operational resilience becomes a standing market in its own right: DORA is no longer just a deadline but a recurring managed-services domain — third-party-risk, resilience testing and the critical-ICT-provider (CTPP) regime — sitting alongside a decade-long core-banking coexistence/integration programme (40% of banks run a modern core beside legacy by 2026, 70-80% by 2028) where services grow faster (~12% CAGR) than licences and the integrator owns the plumbing the SaaS-core vendors don't. Tokenization arrives in bankable form: MiCA is fully binding, a 12-bank consortium (Qivalis) launches a regulated euro stablecoin in H2 2026, the ECB's Pontes DLT settlement rail goes live Q3 2026, and tokenized assets plausibly reach USD 2T (McKinsey base) to USD 9-16T (BCG) by 2030 — pulling custody, key-management and on-chain monitoring into mainstream banking. The durable competitive position belongs to whoever operates the regulated rails — verification, identity acceptance, real-time fraud, AI governance, crypto-agility, resilience and shared compliance utilities — as managed services across many markets, with CEE/SEE's catch-up curves the steepest in the footprint. Cash and ATMs remain a defensible managed-services annuity, but they are the legacy base to optimize, never the growth spine.

drivers.title: The 2027 regulatory wall — but dates slip
drivers.detail: A stacked, dated mandate hits every regulated entity at once: AMLR and Verification-of-Payee from Jul 2027, EUDI wallet acceptance from 6 Dec 2027, AI Act high-risk from Dec 2027 (Aug 2028 embedded), and PQC migration of critical financial systems by end-2030 — converting compliance from a legal project into a permanent, board-level spend line. The hedge: regulators routinely slip (EUDI may drift to ~2032), so the winning posture is selling readiness and managed compliance, not betting on any single date landing on schedule.

drivers.title: Real-time data and the financial-crime/fraud layer
drivers.detail: Instant payments become the legislated default (EU volume ~10x from ~3bn (2024) to ~30bn by 2028; non-euro CEE bound by 9 Jul 2027), killing batch screening and forcing inline VoP, perpetual KYC and ISO 20022 — which splits into TWO revenue pools: real-time fraud orchestration (market USD 32bn to ~66bn by 2030, the fastest near-term ROI for buyers) and a structured-DATA product line (reconciliation, cash-flow forecasting, liquidity/treasury analytics sold off the rail), not merely a Nov-2025/2026 migration deadline.

drivers.title: AI everywhere, governed
drivers.detail: Banking AI software spend rises EUR 31bn (2024) to EUR 55bn (2027) and agentic AI moves into fraud, service and ops — but with >40% of agentic projects cancelled by 2027, durable money migrates to the governance, model-risk and conformity-assurance scaffolding the AI Act mandates, sold to the CRO and model-risk function rather than the channels team.

drivers.title: The endpoint, core and resilience as a service
drivers.detail: Value decouples from boxes and licences toward recurring contracts: ATM-as-a-Service grows ~3x the device market (USD 9bn (2025) to 22bn by 2035), core modernization is a decade-long coexistence programme (40% sidecar by 2026, 70-80% by 2028) where services outgrow licences (~12% CAGR), and DORA turns operational resilience — third-party-risk, resilience testing, CTPP oversight — into a standing managed-services domain, pushing the customer-facing operating layer to whoever runs the managed rails.

gems.title: The long-tail obligated relying party (beyond banks and the 12 sectors)
gems.detail: eIDAS-2 forces every party legally obliged to use strong user authentication to accept the EU Digital Identity Wallet by ~6 Dec 2027 — and the obligation is explicitly NOT limited to the 12 named sectors (telecom, energy, transport, health, etc.). It reaches ANY firm contractually bound to strong authentication (Art. 5f). The named-vendor scramble (Hopae, Lissi, Digidentity, Signicat) targets banks and large platforms; what stays under-served is the long tail of obligated-but-unequipped buyers — regional transport operators, municipal utilities, iGaming/age-gated platforms, MVNOs, mid-market e-commerce — that carry a hard legal acceptance duty but have no identity/compliance team to build verifier integration. The intermediary construct (Art. 5b(10): an intermediary acting for relying parties is itself a relying party) is what lets an integrator like Printec sell acceptance-as-a-service to many such clients off one registration. Inflection window: wallets live 31 Dec 2026, acceptance mandatory ~6 Dec 2027 — a 2027-2030 onboarding wave concentrated in entities that today have no plan. Caveat: the intermediary role itself is already a contested, well-named market; the edge is the buyer segment, not the role.
gems.tag: New buyer: long-tail obligated relying parties with no identity team

gems.title: Operationalising AI Act self-attestation inside CEE/SEE lending stacks
gems.detail: Annex III 5(b) makes credit-scoring AI high-risk with CONTINUOUS, self-attested obligations under internal control (Art.43/Annex VI — no notified body): automatic event logging with 6-month retention (Art.12), meaningful human oversight (Art.14), a quality-management system (Art.17) and ongoing post-market monitoring. The Digital Omnibus deferral (standalone HRAIS to 2 Dec 2027; Annex-I-embedded to 2 Aug 2028, with a Commission early-trigger if standards land sooner) opens a 2026-2027 readiness window. The non-obvious opening is not selling a generic governance SaaS — that market is already crowded (Gartner's first AI Governance MQ, Jun 2026; Credo AI, Holistic AI, Modulos). It is OPERATIONALISING the regime inside the credit-decisioning stack of governance-laggard CEE/SEE lenders: instrumenting their existing scoring engines for logging/oversight/monitoring and producing the recurring self-attestation evidence pack — work Western vendors and Big-4 do not reach but where Printec already holds the integrator relationship. Sold to the CRO / model-risk function as a recurring annuity, not a one-off legal project.
gems.tag: New buyer: CRO / model-risk (continuous self-attestation annuity, not one-off audit)

gems.title: Neutral operator for an Article 75 AML data-sharing utility
gems.detail: AMLR Article 75 makes bank-to-bank "partnerships for information sharing" (PfIS) applicable EU-wide from 10 Jul 2027 — the harmonised legal basis that was missing when GDPR sank the data-centralising TMNL model in 2024. The compliance crowd (Lucinity, Fenergo, Wodan AI, Consilient) is racing to own the analytics/PET layer (federated learning, FHE, secure enclaves that compute without copying data). The under-served slot is the one Printec already fills in shared ATM/cash networks: the NEUTRAL OPERATOR who runs the shared infrastructure and orchestration so a consortium of competing banks can participate without any single bank — or analytics vendor — holding the keys. That trusted-integrator role for a regulated cross-bank AML utility is a new buyer (bank consortium) and a new product line, triggered by a hard 2027 date and validated by TMNL's failure mode (centralisation, not collaboration, was the problem).
gems.tag: New buyer: bank consortium — neutral AML-utility operator

gems.title: Post-quantum crypto discovery and HSM migration
gems.detail: Two hard deadlines converge on the 2027-2030 window: NIST deprecates RSA/ECC after 2030 (disallowed 2035), and the EU's coordinated roadmap (NIS Cooperation Group, 2025) asks member states to stand up cryptographic inventories by end-2026 and migrate critical financial systems to post-quantum cryptography by end-2030 — yet most banks still cannot say where cryptography actually runs in their estate and file quantum under "future research." The near-term billable wedge is discovery: building the cryptographic bill-of-materials (CBOM) that regulators are starting to require. The follow-on is a 3-5 year crypto-agile HSM and key-lifecycle refresh, the most hardware-intensive part of the migration. Crucially this is a horizontal security-architecture practice — the buyer is the CISO/security-architecture team, not Printec's usual cash/branch buyer — and the same discovery-and-refresh motion reaches telecom, eID/digital-identity and utilities, all named secondary PQC markets sustaining demand into the 2030s.
gems.tag: New line: PQC discovery and HSM migration

gems.title: The PSD3/MiCA re-authorisation cohort as a net-new stack buyer
gems.detail: Non-banks are the fastest-growing core-banking buyer cohort (~14.8% CAGR to 2031 per Mordor/Straits, vs banks at 73% of the 2025 base) — BNPL providers, EMIs, embedded-finance brands and MiCA CASPs that sit entirely outside the traditional bank-account list. A concrete 2027-2030 catalyst makes them addressable on a deadline rather than as a vague trend: PSD3 merges the PI and EMI regimes into a single payment institution with a ~24-month re-authorisation window (core obligations land H2 2027), and the EBA's 2025 No-Action Letter plus the Feb 2026 Opinion push CASPs handling fiat payments toward PSD3 authorisation. This forces a fixed, named cohort to re-platform onboarding/KYC, AML, secure key management/HSM and card-issuing enablement fast, with no in-house integration team. The opportunity for Printec is the integration, orchestration and managed-service layer around that regulated stack (not building a proprietary core), sold to a buyer it has never invoiced before.
gems.tag: New buyer on a regulatory deadline: PSD3 PI/EMI + MiCA CASP cohort

source_note: Figures trace to consulting houses (McKinsey, Gartner, Capgemini, Deloitte, BCG, Everest, IDC), EU and central-bank sources (ECB, EBA, ESMA, AMLA, European Commission, NIST/NIS Cooperation Group), market-sizing firms (MarketsandMarkets, Mordor/Straits, Grand View, Juniper) and vendor/regulatory guidance; TARGET2/TIPS access traces to the amended Settlement Finality Directive plus the 2025 EBA/ECB/NCB MoU. All market sizes and adoption curves are projections where labelled, span different end-years (several extend to 2031 or 2035), and vary by analyst; regulatory dates are subject to slippage.
